props.title: Perfect Sense
props.initialSlug: When the senses vanish, love endures.

sections.content: **Perfect Sense (2011)** (2011) stands among the most unique pandemic films ever made, following a global epidemic where humans gradually lose their senses one by one. Unlike typical virus thrillers like **Contagion** (2011) or **Outbreak** (1995), it's an intimate drama starring Ewan McGregor and Eva Green as lovers finding connection while humanity adapts to each sensory loss. The film haunts with its premise - first smell disappears, then taste, creating waves of panic before people adjust to their new normal. Director David Mackenzie crafts something between science fiction and romance, closer in spirit to **Children of Men** (2006) than traditional disaster films.

sections.content: What makes **Perfect Sense** particularly relevant is how it portrays collective trauma and adaptation. Like **Melancholia** (2011) and **Take Shelter** (2011), it's less interested in the mechanics of disaster than in human psychology facing inevitable loss. The film's genius lies in showing how people find new ways to experience joy - when taste disappears, texture becomes everything; when hearing goes, touch intensifies. It's a meditation on human resilience that feels especially poignant post-COVID.

The film's approach to romance amid catastrophe shares DNA with **Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind** (2004) and **Never Let Me Go** (2010) - intimate stories set against science fiction backdrops. Director Mackenzie avoids typical apocalyptic imagery, instead focusing on quiet moments of connection and adaptation. The restaurant scenes, where chefs including McGregor's character reinvent food for a tasteless world, are particularly powerful. SUBHEAD: The New Wave of Intimate Apocalypse Films

movies.title: It Comes at Night
movies.slug: A family maintains strict rules to survive an unnamed plague, but their orderly world unravels when they take in another family.

sections.content: **Perfect Sense** helped pioneer what we might call the "intimate apocalypse" genre, followed by films like **Arrival** (2016) and **Bird Box** (2018). These films use global catastrophe as backdrop rather than centerpiece, examining personal relationships under extreme pressure. Like **A Quiet Place** (2018), they show how crisis forces humans to develop new ways of connecting and communicating.
